newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW-HELSINKI BOURSE HOPES TO MAINTAIN VOLUME.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-HELSINKI BOURSE HOPES TO MAINTAIN VOLUME.

text.p: The Helsinki Stock Exchange expects to maintain the volumes next year even after posting record trade volumes and new highs for shares in 1996, managing director Juhani Erma said on Tuesday.
"At the moment things look good; even if we don't break any records, the level will at least be maintained," he told Reuters in an interview.
Further ahead, Helsinki aims to remain the best market for Finnish shares in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) but has yet to define a cooperation strategy, Erma said.
Volume on the smallest Nordic exchange set a new record already by November 12 as the value of trade in shares rose just above the previous 83 billion markka record from last year.

By last Friday, trade was worth 96.5 billion markka, still clearly behind Oslo's at the equivalent of over 150 billion markka -- though Oslo has a slightly smaller total market capitalisation than Helsinki.

Stockholm is the Nordic region's biggest bourse with a domestic market capitalisation of some 1,081 billion markka compared to Helsinki's 270 billion at end-November, and volume at the equivalent of 573 billion markka.

Finnish share prices have set life-highs and the HEX index has added 40 percent this year to new records, but Erma said he did not believe this year's trading interest has been extraordinary in any way.
"It has been rather natural trade," he said.

On future cooperation, Erma said he would prefer this to be based on links for trade between bourses, making possible trade on other exchanges via a home terminal, rather than tighter options like joint trading.

"I think (trading links) are the basis to start building cooperation on," he said. "A trade on one exchange in another country's stock would automatically be registered in the home exchange," he said.

The bourse estimates that 50 percent or more of daily volumes are dealings by international investors, and the partly or wholly foreign-owned brokerages in Helsinki have a joint market share of some 50 percent, he said.

Joint trading would probably give the most benefits from cooperation, but this would be very hard to achieve since it would require coordinating systems, rules and legislation, he said -- setting up trading links would not require that.
Erma said the issue of whom to ally with was open as well.

Nordic bourses would be natural partners -- but with Finland keen to be in the first stage of Economic and Monetary Union and Sweden and Denmark less so, joining with them is not obvious even though Stockholm plans to quote prices in euro, he said.
And the Stockholm exchange's wish to be the main Nordic market is continues to make its smaller neighbours wary.
"It is a problem when someone says they should be the key market," Erma said.
Cooperation between other bourses in Europe has not yet found its form and it is too early to say where interest in Finnnish stocks would come from in the single currency area, he added.
"It's all still open ... but the Nordic countries would be the closest."

The Helsinki bourse has defined a strategic aim to be "the best market for Finnish companies' shares" and to be an attractive option for the region. "Only the few largest of our companies could make it without a home bourse," Erma said.
In addition to suiting Finnish companies, Helsinki could offer better access to international capital and better trading technology for instance to Estonian firms, he said.
